level1.text: A magnetic resonance imaging scanner in a hospital has a magnetic flux density of $3.0\,\text{T}$. The magnetic flux density of the Earth's magnetic field is about $50\,\mu\text{T}$. How many times greater is the field of the scanner than the Earth's field?

In Kuopio the magnetic flux density of the Earth's magnetic field is about $53\,\mu\text{T}$, and the field points $75^\circ$ below the horizontal. What is the horizontal component of the field in microtesla?

At a compass the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field is $14\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the north and the field of a magnet on the table is $48\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the east. What is the horizontal total field in microtesla?
A bar magnet is cut in two in the middle. What poles does each piece have? Do the pieces attract or repel each other when the cut faces are brought back together?
level1.answer: Each piece has a north pole and a south pole. The cut faces have unlike poles, so the pieces attract each other.

level1.text: A compass is placed on a table on the axis of a bar magnet in front of the north pole $\text{N}$ of the magnet. The Earth's field is ignored. Which way does the north end of the compass needle point, and why?
level1.answer: Away from the magnet: the field of the magnet points away from the north pole, and the north pole of the needle repels the north pole of the magnet.

level1.text: A magnet attracts an iron nail but not an aluminium can or a copper coin. Which of the following explains the difference?
level1.answer: Iron is ferromagnetic, so its magnetic domains align in the field of the magnet; aluminium and copper are not.

choices.text: Iron conducts electricity better than aluminium and copper, so the field of the magnet makes more current flow in iron.
choices.feedback: Wrong: electrical conductivity does not decide it. Copper conducts electricity even better than iron, yet a magnet does not attract it. What matters is whether the substance is ferromagnetic.

choices.text: Iron is denser and heavier than aluminium, so a magnet attracts only heavier pieces of metal.
choices.feedback: Wrong: magnetic interaction does not depend on mass or density. Copper is even denser than iron, and a magnet still does not attract it. What matters is whether the substance is ferromagnetic.

choices.text: Iron is ferromagnetic, so its magnetic domains align in the field of the magnet; aluminium and copper are not.
choices.feedback: Correct: a magnet attracts only ferromagnetic substances, such as iron, nickel and cobalt. The magnetic domains of iron align in the field of the magnet, and the substance becomes magnetised. Aluminium and copper have no such domains.

choices.text: The atomic dipoles of aluminium and copper cancel each other completely, whereas iron has no magnetic atomic dipoles at all.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the atoms of iron have magnetic dipoles, and they form domains that point the same way. This is exactly what makes iron ferromagnetic. The claim is the opposite of the truth.

level1.text: The north end of a compass needle points roughly towards the geographic north. The Earth's field is described as the field of a bar magnet. What does the direction of the needle tell about the poles of this model?
level1.answer: In the bar-magnet model there is a south pole near the geographic North Pole, because the north pole of the needle is attracted by an unlike pole.

choices.text: In the bar-magnet model there is a north pole near the geographic North Pole, because the north pole of the needle seeks a pole of the same name.
choices.feedback: Wrong: poles of the same name repel each other, so the north end of the needle does not seek a north pole. It points towards an unlike pole, that is, the south pole of the bar-magnet model.

choices.text: The needle points north because the rotation of the Earth turns a light needle along the axis of rotation, and the magnetic field has no part in it.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the needle of a compass is a magnet, and it is turned by the Earth's magnetic field. It would work the same way even if the Earth did not rotate, and it points towards a magnetic pole, not along the axis of rotation.

choices.text: The Earth's magnetic field has no poles, so the needle points north only because of gravity and the friction of the bearing.
choices.feedback: Wrong: the Earth's field resembles the field of a bar magnet, and it has a pole at each end. The needle is turned by magnetic interaction, not by gravity or friction.

choices.text: In the bar-magnet model there is a south pole near the geographic North Pole, because the north pole of the needle is attracted by an unlike pole.
choices.feedback: Correct: the north end of the needle is the north pole of a magnet, and unlike poles attract each other. Since the north end of the needle points towards the geographic north, the south pole of the bar-magnet model is there. In geomagnetism this pole is nevertheless called the magnetic north pole.

level1.text: In Oulu the magnetic flux density of the Earth's magnetic field is about $53\,\mu\text{T}$, and the field points $76\,{}^\circ$ below the horizontal. What is the vertical component of the field in microtesla?

A student examines a bar magnet on a table; its ends are marked with the poles $\text{N}$ and $\text{S}$. The student uses a compass and iron filings and records five statements about the observations. Near the magnet the Earth's magnetic field is much weaker than the field of the magnet.

Decide which statements are true and which are false.

statements.text: When a short piece is sawn off the $\text{N}$ end of the magnet, the long piece that remains has only a south pole $\text{S}$.
statements.feedback: False: the poles of a magnet always occur in pairs. A new north pole forms at the cut, so the long piece still has both $\text{N}$ and $\text{S}$, and so does the short piece.

statements.text: Next to the side of the magnet, at its middle, the north end of a compass needle points towards the $\text{N}$ end of the magnet.
statements.feedback: False: outside the magnet the field lines go from the north pole to the south pole. Next to the side the field therefore points towards the $\text{S}$ end, and the north end of the needle turns in the direction of the field.

statements.text: Inside the magnet the field lines go from the south pole to the north pole, so every field line is a closed loop.
statements.feedback: True: outside the lines go from $\text{N}$ to $\text{S}$ and inside from $\text{S}$ to $\text{N}$. A line has no beginning and no end, because there is no single magnetic pole.

statements.text: When the magnet is hung from a thread so that it can turn freely, its $\text{N}$ end turns towards the Earth's magnetic south pole.
statements.feedback: True: unlike poles attract each other, so the $\text{N}$ end turns towards the Earth's magnetic south pole. It is near the geographic north pole, so the $\text{N}$ end points north.

statements.text: When a second magnet is brought onto the table, the field lines of the two magnets can cross each other between them.
statements.feedback: False: the field is the vector sum of the fields of the two magnets, and at each point it has only one direction. Therefore the field lines of the total field never cross each other.

level2.text: The field of a magnet at a compass is $25\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the east, and the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field is $14\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the north. Through how many degrees does the compass needle turn from north towards east?

The magnetometer application of a smartphone shows the components of the Earth's magnetic field $B_x = 12\,\mu\text{T}$, $B_y = -5.0\,\mu\text{T}$ and $B_z = -48\,\mu\text{T}$. The components are perpendicular to each other. What is the magnetic flux density of the Earth's magnetic field in microtesla?

In Rovaniemi the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is about $52\,\mu\text{T}$, and the field points $77^\circ$ below the horizontal. What is the magnetic flux density of the field in microtesla?

A compass is on the axis of a magnet, and the field of the magnet is perpendicular to the horizontal component of the Earth's field. When the compass is $10\,\text{cm}$ from the magnet, the needle turns $60^\circ$ from north. When it is $20\,\text{cm}$ away, the needle turns $10^\circ$. How many times greater is the field of the magnet at $10\,\text{cm}$ than at $20\,\text{cm}$?

A compass is on the axis of a bar magnet, east of the magnet, and the field of the magnet points east at the compass. The horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field is $14\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the north. The table gives the angle through which the compass needle turns from north when the distance of the compass from the magnet is $r$ (example data).

a) Calculate the magnetic flux density $B_\text{m}$ of the magnet at a distance of $12\,\text{cm}$.

b) Calculate $B_\text{m}$ also at distances of $8.0\,\text{cm}$ and $16\,\text{cm}$. Is the field inversely proportional to the distance? Justify by comparing how the field changes when the distance doubles.

Enter the result of part a) in microtesla in the answer field.

level2.text:
The components of the magnetic flux density were measured with the magnetometer of a smartphone in three places in the same room (example data). The phone was held in the same orientation every time, and the components are perpendicular to each other. The Earth's field in this room is about $50\,\mu\text{T}$.

a) Calculate the total field in each place.

b) In which place is there probably iron or steel nearby? Justify.

Enter in the answer field the total field next to the desk from part a) in microtesla.

A student solves the problem: “At a compass the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field is $14\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the north and the field of a magnet on the table is $30\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the east. Through how many degrees does the needle turn from north towards east?”

Their solution: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{B_\text{h}}{B_\text{m}} = \dfrac{14\,\mu\text{T}}{30\,\mu\text{T}} = 0.467$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1} 0.467 = 25\,{}^\circ$.

a) Why is the result implausible when the field of the magnet is much greater than the Earth's field? What is the mistake in the solution?

b) Calculate the correct angle.

Enter the result of part b) in degrees in the answer field.

level3.text: A bar magnet lies on a table in the north–south direction with its north pole $\text{N}$ towards the north. A compass is placed east of the magnet at the level of the middle of the magnet, where the field of the magnet is $25\,\mu\text{T}$. The horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field is $14\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the north. Calculate the north component of the horizontal total field in microtesla, with north as the positive direction and south as the negative. Which way does the north end of the compass needle point?

A steel paper clip is drawn several times in the same direction along a pole of a magnet, after which it picks up small pins. When the clip is heated in a flame hot enough and allowed to cool, it no longer picks up pins. Explain both observations using magnetic domains.
level3.answer: The field of a magnet aligns the magnetic domains of the steel, and in hard steel they stay aligned, so the clip is a magnet. Heating to a high enough temperature mixes up the alignment of the domains, so the clip is no longer a magnet.

level3.text:
According to the model of the Earth's magnetic field (World Magnetic Model 2025) the field in Helsinki is about $53\,\mu\text{T}$ and points about $74^\circ$ below the horizontal. In Longyearbyen in Svalbard the field is about $55\,\mu\text{T}$ and points about $82.5^\circ$ below the horizontal.

How many times greater is the horizontal component of the field in Helsinki than in Longyearbyen? Why does a compass work worse in Longyearbyen, although the whole field is greater there?

The table gives the magnetic flux density $B$ of the Earth's magnetic field and the inclination $I$, that is, the direction of the field below the horizontal, in three towns (example data, close to the values of the World Magnetic Model). In each town the same bar magnet is placed next to a compass so that its field at the compass is $20\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the east.

a) Calculate the horizontal component of the Earth's field in each town.

b) Calculate the angle through which the compass needle turns from north towards east in each town.

c) The total field is almost the same in all the towns. Explain why the turning angle of the needle nevertheless grows as one goes north, and what this tells about the operation of a compass in the north.

Enter the result of part b) for Utsjoki in the answer field.

level3.text:
A researcher measures the field of a bar magnet as a function of distance with a compass. The magnet lies in the east–west direction east of the compass, on its axis, with its south pole towards the compass, so its field points east at the compass. The horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field is $14\,\mu\text{T}$ towards the north. The table gives the angle through which the needle turns from north when the distance of the compass from the magnet is $r$ (example data).

a) Calculate the magnetic flux density $B_\text{m}$ of the magnet at each point and show that the product $B_\text{m} r^3$ is approximately constant.

b) The magnet is turned to the north–south direction and placed north of the compass, on its axis, with its north pole towards the compass. Assume that the field of the magnet at the compass is as great as the table gives for the same distance on the axis. At what distance $r_0$ is the horizontal total field zero, so that the needle does not settle in any direction?

c) Which way does the north end of the needle point when the distance is less than $r_0$, and which way when it is greater? Justify.

Enter the result of part b) in centimetres in the answer field.
